author: Brother Aldo, formerly of the Hill Shrine
pages:
#I Was Paid to Look the Other Way

I kept a small shrine to the Divines on the high road for nineteen years. I lit the candles, swept the steps and blessed travellers who left a coin in the bowl. It was honest work, and I was proud of it.

What follows is not honest, and I am not proud of it, but I am told that confession is good for the soul.

#The Visitor

In my twelfth year a woman in a grey hood came to the shrine at midnight. She asked whether the cellar beneath the altar was in use. It was not. She offered me a purse of gold to forget that she had asked.

I took it. Gold is very persuasive to a man who eats turnips five days a week.

#What Happened Below

After that, people came and went beneath my shrine every new moon. I heard chanting through the floorboards. I smelled things burning that were not incense. Once I heard laughter that did not sound like it came from any human throat.

I told myself it was not my business. I lit my candles a little brighter and sang my hymns a little louder.

#The Night It Ended

One night the chanting stopped mid-word, and there was a sound like a great door slamming somewhere very far below. The next morning the cellar was empty, scorched black, and the woman in grey never returned.

The candles on my altar would not stay lit after that. I left the shrine the following spring.

#My Penance

I now walk the roads and warn shrine-keepers to check their cellars. Most of them laugh at me. A few have gone quiet and pale, and I know they have their own woman in grey.

If you are one of them: it is not too late to stop taking the gold.
